RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
Statement 
(a) to (d) During 23rd—25th March, 2005. The Centre for Economic and Social Studies 
(CESS), an autonomous institution, organized a South Asia Regional Conference on the 
subject, "Globalization of Agriculture in South Asia: Has it Made a Difference to Rural 
Livelihoods?". As part of this conference on 25th March, 2005, a Round Table meeting of 
Agriculture Ministers/key policy makers of South Asian Countries was organized on, 
"Prospects for South Asia Free Trade and Cooperation in Agriculture Sector". 
Representatives from India, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Pakistan participated in the 
round table meeting. 
The aforementioned meeting was not an official inter-Govemmental meeting. A wide 
range of issues pertaining to the agnculture sector were discussed. 
The major recommendations were: 
(i) Public investment should be increased in agriculture sector. 
(ii) A South Asia Free Trade Regional Block (SAFTRB) should be formed for 
the select agricultural commodities where both importer and exporter have 
comparative advantage. 
(iii) The farm products where the current applied duty in SAARC region is 
already equal to its WTO bound rate, may be protected. 
(iv) The interest of small farmers in the globalised environment may be protected. 
(v) The SAARC countries need to take a proactive stand in WTO by asking for 
reduction of subsidies and increasing market access for these countries. 
          (vi) Infrastructure development in rural areas, diversification of                                 
agriculture towards high value added products, development of                    
institutions especially in insurance, futures trading and contract                    
farming, regulation of retail markets and development of sanitary and phyto-
sanitary standards. 
The issues relevant to the WTO have been taken up in the on-going negotiations. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Sir, agriculture growth in India between 1986 and 
1995 was 3.2 per cent, but suddenly between 1996 and 2003,— 
2 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
in seven years—it came down to 1.5 per cent. There has been an adverse impact on 
agriculture sector and rural livelihood. I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister how it has gone down so considerably, and what the Minister, the 
Government, is planning to increase it to make a comeback to 3.2 per cent or 
more. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, there are a number of reasons, but, in fact, 
the overall position is not that bad. If you study the provisions that were exactly 
made in the last 5-7 years, you will find that the total budgetary provision to this 
entire sector was below 2 per cent—it was between 1.30 and 1.45 at the 
maximum. It has definitely affected. 
Secondly, the public investment in agriculture sector was day-by-day 
decreasing. Take the case of irrigation sector. In this Budget, there has been a 
substantial improvement. Prior to this, in the last three years, the total provision 
for irrigation sector was less than 0.35 per cent, not even one per cent and not even 
half per cent. It was somewhat nearly 0.35 per cent, and that has definitely affected 
it. I would like to take the entire House into confidence that till last year, or the 
year before the last year, the budgetary provision for drought was much more than the 
budgetary provision for irrigation and ultimately that has affected, but corrective 
action has been taken. For instance, last year, the budgetary provision for 
irrigation was somewhat near to Rs. 2,200 crores, and this year it has jumped to 
Rs. 4,000 crores. डबल से भी Ïयादा हो गयी । A substantial improvement in there. 
The total provision for irrigation has been improved from Rs. 2,400 crores to 
somewhat near to Rs. 4,000 crores. That is si definite improvement. These types of 
corrective actions are definitely taken, and along with this, a substantial 
improvement is also made this year in the area of agriculture credit. As I have 
already disclosed this information to the House, till last year, the total money which 
was disbursed for agricultural credit was somewhat near to Rs. 80,000 crores. 
This year, we have crossed Rs. 1,15,000 crores. This type of jump in difinitely there, 
and it will continue. It will take 2-3 years to make an overall improvement, and I 
am confident that the UPA Government's total approach is to give a lot of weightage 
and importance to the agriculture sector, and these types of corrective actions 
will be taken.

plans to improve our policy regarding the WTO. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Initially, when we got a request from this 
particular organisation, there was a communication that Agriculture Ministers 
from Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Pakistan are also going to participate. So, I 
accepted that invitation. To be very frank, Ministers only from Bhutan and India

conclusion of that conference. We thought if the neighbouring countries are 
seriously thinking about these WTO problems, we should associate themselves

to protect the interests of the Indian farming community. That is the reason why

SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Sir, with regard to the expansion of 
agriculture, nowadays, the food processing is very important and in advanced 
countries, they are sending the processed food at highly competitive prices.

competitive price of the processed food which would be more helpful to the 
farmers. What are the steps taken by the Government in this regard? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: This is one of the areas where we have to take a 
lot of interest and we have to give a lot of support. As I have disclosed this 
information on some other occasion in the House, one of the major problems 
which the Indian agriculture faces is post-harvesting losses. Unless and until, 
we improve this infrastructure, unless and until, we set up and encourage the 
agro-processed industries thoughout India, we will not be able to reduce these 
post-harvesting losses. As I have already given the figures, the last year's total 
post-harvesting loss in this counry was somewhat Rs. 50.000 crores. India is 
one of the countries, to be frank, which have neglected it. Even small countries 
like Philippines and Thailand are also doing much better than us. These are the 
countries which are practically processing more than 60 to 70 per cent of their 
agricultural produce; as against in India, we have not reached even two per cent. 
That is why, this Ministry is taking a lot of interest and a lot of initiatives are 
being taken up.

*609. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

(a) whether Government have recognized.'Naturopath/ as a system of medicine;

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences is actively engaged in 
research and therapeutic procedure involving the use of various stem cells. The treatment 
offered at AIIMS is free to the patients so far. Since the procedures are carried out as 
part of overall research activity and are at initial stage, the exact cost per patient are 
yet to be worked out. There is also no.discrimination between the rich and poor, in 
providing this treatment and decision is made after careful evaluation of the specific needs 
of the patient. 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Sir, I would like to congratulate the .hon. 
Minister for the poineering work done by the AIIMS. I would also like to congratulate the 
Director of AIIMS, Shri Venugopal, in whom we have a very dedicated doctor and an 
able administrator. I would like to know from hon. Minister as to how the Government 
plans to support and further enhance the stem cells intiatives in AIIMS in terms of 
manpower, funds and other means whatsoever. 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMADOSS: Sir, the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences, a poineer research institute in the country, has been carrying out various 
research projects, including the stem cell research. In the last so many years, they have 
been focusing on cardiac stem cells research, 
18 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
research on eyes and pancreatic stem ce ll research. All this research is being 
done. 
Sir, there are three types of stem cells. I would like, through you, Sir, to just 
enlighten the House about stem cells. There are three types of stem cells. One is 
the adult stem cell, found in the adult bone marrow, tissues and muscles. The 
second is the umbilican chord stem cells, found during delivery. There are stem 
cells in the umbilical, chord. The third is the embryonic stem cell; during the 
fifth and the seventh day, when the embryo is formed, you get those cells and you 
propogate those cells. So, there are these three types of stem cells. 
In the case of embryonic stem cell research in the developed countries, they are 
facing a problem pertaining to ethical values because some of these embryonic 
cells could become cancerous cells in future by mutation. In the case of adult stem 
cells, there is no such problem. At AIIMS, the autologous cells, i.e., patient's 
own cells, were injected just like blood transfusion. So, during a heart surgery, 
when the heart is opened, sternum cells are taken out, stem cells are identified, 
and then they were again in jected indirectly into the heart muscles where, in 
certain patients, it started growing and their recovery was better than other 
patients. This research is still going.on in the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences, including the Rajendra Prasad  Eye Centre where the corneal cells 
are also used for research purposes. 
The Government is very actively involved in propagating the stem cells 
research in the country because this is going to be a big future in the medicine, 
because in a short span of time, I am sure, Sir, the world over all the organs in the 
body could be grown to get treatment for diabetes, spinal chord problems, in 
muscular dystrophy and cancer. So, this is a huge initiative that the 
Government has taken through the Department of Biotechnology and the 
Department of Science and Technology. We are propagating this in a big way, 
nationally. We have put in a lot of resources in the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences. They have formed a separate banking for these chord cells and other 
cells and we are propagating that and we are helping them in a big way. 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Sir, the Minister has talked about

research in foetal and chord blood cells.

†*614. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govemment have carried out any enquiry into the health related 
aspects and arrangements/facilities at national level in urban and rural areas; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the number of such hospitals where even doctors/staff are not available; 
(d) whether Govemment carry out study about the spread of new diseases in 
those areas; and 
(e) if so, the measures taken for prevention and protection of such areas in 
future? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) A Facility Survey has be en conducted in the country, in two 
phases (1998-99 and 2003-2004), which assessed the availability of infrastructure i.e. 
water facility, electricity, vehicle, operation theatre, labour room etc. and helath 
manpower position in the Primary Health Care Institutions in the country. 
With a view to creating a comprehensive demographic and health database in 
India, National Family Health Survey s were conducted during the year 
1992-93 and Second Round in 1998-99. 
With a view to assess the impact of RCH Programme, it was necessary to 
generate district level data on the utilization of services provided by government 
health facilities, other than service statistics. A Rapid Household Survey (RHS) in all 
the districts of the of the country in two round, 50 percent of the districts were 
covered in the first phase of the project in 1998-99. In the first round, 50 percent of the 
districts were covered in the first phase of the project in 1998 and thereafter, the 
remaining 50 percent districts were covered under second phase in 1999. 
In addition, National Council of Applied Economics Research (NCAER) 
carried out the evaluation of Sub-centres in selected districts of the country to 
assess the performance of the sub-centre s with respect to availability of 
infrastructure, manpower, equipment, medicines, efficacy of service delivery, 
extent of coordination and to understand the impact of the Family Welfare 
Programme. The Data has been collected from 1040 sub-centres in 130 districts 
covering 30% of the districts of 14 major States in India. 
The Rural Health Care Infrastructure status in the country is also being 
monitored through regional workshops. Four such workshops were held at 
Chandigarh, Chennai, Mumbai and Kolkata in November-December, 2004.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) As per Section 12Aof the Homoeopathy Central Council (Amendment)

(b) The CCH has been constituted under Section, 3(1) of the 
Homoeopathy Central Council Act, 1973. The main functions of the Council 
are to prescribe minimum standards of education in Homoeopathy, maintain, 
a Central register of practitioners of Homoeopathy, prescribe standards of 
professional conduct or etiquette and code of ethics for Homoeopathy, 
removal of any person from the Central Register, if the person enrolled on 
a State Register of Homoeopathy is removed therefrom in pursuance of 
any power under any law relating to registration of practitioners and make 
regulations with the previous sanction of the Central Government to carry 
out the purposes of the Homoeopathic Central Council Act. The term of 
President, Vice President or a Member of the Council is five years from 
the date of his election and nomination or till his successor is duly elected 
or nominated, whichever is longer. There is no express provision in the law 
for their suspension. Suspension orders for the Group 'C and 'D' employees 
of the Council are passed by the Secretary, CCH. Similar authority is 
exercised in respect of Office Superi ntendent and Assistant Secretary by 
the President and for Secretary by the Executive Committee of the Council.

MNCs' Monopoly in grain market 
†*610. SHRI SURENDRALATH:  
              SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
(a) whether it is a fact that sale and purchase of foodgrains is undertaken in India 
through markets meant for it, whereas MNCs are trying to establish their monopoly 
over grain market by distorting agricultural marketing laws and driving wedge 
into markets; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that E-chaupal of ITC in Madhya Pradesh 
is an example of this move and whether establishment of monopolies of MNCs 
in the grain markets would not eliminate employment opportunities fully and 
whether the farmers of the country would not become bonded labourers; and 
(c) if so, the remedial measures being taken by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) Sale 
and purchase of foodgrains is undertaken through markets set up by the State 
Governments under the provisions of the Agriculture Produce marketing 
(Regulation) Act (APMC Act). Trade is carried on in the market area under the 
supervision and control of the market Committee set up under the Act. As a 
consequence of the regulation, no other person/ agency can set up market for 
agricultural commodities in notified areas. Processing industries cannot buy directly 
from farmers except through licensed traders and notified markets. Farmers are 
restricted from entering in to a direct contract with any manufacturer as the 
produce is required to be canalized through the regulated markets. These 
restrictions are working as disincentive to farmers, traders and industries. State 
Governments have, therefore, been advised to bring changes in the APMC Act to 
allow direct marketing and contract fa rming, in order to promote competitive 
markets. 
Madhya Pradesh is first amongst the States which have implemented these 
reforms by amending the APMC Act to facilitate direct sale by producer to the 
buyer and firect purchase by the buyer from the producer. A provision is also 
made in the Act for setting up of private market and promotion of direct 
marketing. Farmers have the option to sell his produce either in the nearby mandi 
or at the purchase centers as per his convenience. Thus, there is no monopoly of 
MNCs over the grain markets. 
(b) and (c) E-choupal is a project of ITC Limited, an Indian company, which 
offers farmers the facilities of information dissemination through internet viz. 
farming best practices, weather conditions and prices of various crops; purchase 
of farmers' produce at ITC buying centres approved by respective States'APMC rules 
and selling quality farm inputs and other consumer goods. Farmers are benefited by 
using these facilities. This initiative has provided more freedom to farmer to sell his 
agricultural produce 
40 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to an agency offering better price at his doorstep. Within such an open and 
transparent arrangement there is no question of scope for employment or making 
the farmers bonded labours.

fisherman and resort owners of Goa and North Karnataka. For this, they deployed 
ships ex Mumbai and Goa for assessment and containment operations. The 
CG Dornier aircraft and helicopters were utilized for monitoring of the situation 
and aerial spraying of oil spill dispersant (OSD). The ship borne spill

(c) whether Government would assure of paying the price for cotton growers in 
advance through Mark-fed, which could recover the same amount from the Cotton Corporation of 
India, through an agreement between farmers, Cotton Corporation of India and Mark-fed, to 
solve the present crisis of hardships of cotton growers in getting their price amount

unbearable indebtedness under exploiting private money lenders; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The main objective of price policy for agricultural 
produce is to ensure remunerative prices to the growers for their produce. The Government 
decides on the Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for various agricultural commodities, 
taking into account the recommendations of Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices 
(CACP), the views of State Government and concerned Central Ministries as well as such 
other relevant factors, which in the opinion of the Government, are important for fixation fo 
MSPs. Based on these factors, the Government announced MSPs of Kharif crops of 2005-
06 season on 20th April, 2005. 
Since MSPs do not necessarily exceeds the weighted average C2 cost (actual expenses 
incurred in cash and kind, rent for leased-in land and imputed value of wages of family 
labour, rent for owned land and interest ort fixed capital) in respect of all crops/States, the 
price policy seeks to ensure that the A2+FL cost (actual expenses in cash and kind incurred 
in production + rent paid for leased-in land + imputed value of family labour) is covered by 
MSP in high cost/less endowed States. The weighted average A2+FL?cost of production 
works out to Rs. 1549 per quintal. Thus the MSP of Rs. 1760 per quintal fixed for 2005-06 
for F-414/H-777/J-34 cotton provides adequate margin over the A2+FL cost of production. 
Similarly, in case of groundnut the MSP of Rs. 1520 per quintal provides adequate margin 
over the weighted average A2+FL cost of Rs. 1178 per quintal. In fact, the SP of Rs. 1520 
announced for 2005-06 covers the weighted average C2 cost of Rs. 1509 per 
quintal. 
(c) and (d) The qualify of kapas (i.e. fibre characteristics and grades) brought to the 
market yard is assessed by the buyers, including Cotton Corporation of India (CCI), in 
the market yards in the presence of representatives of Market Committee. After fixing 
of the price, kapa§ is weighed and bills prepared and only then the value of cotton in 
determined. 
65 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
Thus, it is not possible to pay the price to the cotton growers in advance through 
MARK-FED. 
CCI releases payments directly to farmers or to the commission agents within a period of 
7 to 10 days. Some delay may occur due to non-receipt of bills from commission agents or 
delay in weighment in the current cotton season due to unprecedented and massive 
purchases under MSP operations but efforts have been made to release payments as 
quickly as possible. 
Foodgrain Production 
4659. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the foodgrain production to the year 2004-05 is estimated as 
210.44 million tonnes against 213.46 million tonnes last year 
(b) if so, the reason for the shortfall; 
(c) Whether it is also a fact that Government have assessed the rabi prospects and 
discussed the strategies and plans for the coming kharif season including the input 
situation and budget position; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) Yes Sir, The foodgrain production in 2004-05 is 
estimated at 210.44 million tonnes against 213.46 million tonnes last years. The reason of 
the decline is inadequate rainfall received during monsoon 2004. As compared to 2003, the 
southwest monsoon in 
2004 was erratic with prolonged weak/break monsoon conditions prevailing 
during late June, most of July, late August and early September over 
different parts of the country. For the country as a whole, the seasonal 
rainfall from 1st June to 30th Sept ember was 87% of its Long Period 
Average (LPA). As a consequence the kharif foodgrain production in 2004- 
05 declined and is estimated at 104.08 million tonnes which is 12.8 
million tonnes or 10.95% less than the corresponding Kharif production in 
2003-04. However, the rabi production in 2004-05 JS estimated at 106.36 
million tonnes which is 9.78 million tonnes or 10.13% more than the 
corresponding production figure in 2003-04. 
(c) and (d) The National Conference on Agriculture for Kharif Campaign      2005was held 
oh 22nd and 23rd March 2005 at New Delhi to assess the 
66 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Rabi Prospects for 2004-05 and to review preparation for kharif crops of 2005. The 
assessment of Rabi production done in the Conference has been mentioned above. In 
the Conference the Government underscored the importance of integrated efforts by 
Public and Private Institutions like Farmer's Associations, State Agricultural Universities, 
ICAR Institutes, for addressing the challenges confronting the Agriculture Sector. 
The Government has initiated steps to ensure increased credit flow to the rural sector 
and for higher investment in irrigationiacilities and towards better resource conservation 
strategies. Stress has been given to higher seed replacement ratio for hybrid and high 
yielding varieties, setting up of more plant quarantine stations, and Agricultural Clinics 
aimed at promoting self employment of agricultural graduates, increased efforts in soil 
mapping for dry land rainfed areas and de-centralizing extension facilities at district and 
block levels. 
Regarding Agricultural inputs, like quality seeds, fertilizers etc. efforts are on to

4662. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will th e Minister of AGRICULTURE be

target of 4.0 per cent;

(c) whether it is also a fact that Government had decided to reverse the

(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. According to the data released by 
Central Statistical Organization (CSO), the growth rate in agriculture, including 
allied sectors of forestry & logging, and fishing, was negative (-7%) in 2002-
03 while it was 9.6% in 2003-04. According to the advance estimates released by 
the CSO, growth rate in agriculture, including allied sectors, in 2004-05 is 1.1%. 
The average annual growth rate for the first three years of the Tenth Plan 
works out to 1.2%.

production, is heavily influenced by rainfall. The year 2002-03 witnessed a severe 
drought that affected several States in the country. The favourable rainfall from 
the southwest monsoon in 2003-04 boosted agricultural production. However, 
the rainfall from the south-west monsoon in the year 2004-05 was deficient 
across time and space. Though the deficien cy in rainfall from the south-west 
monsoon in 2004 was less serious than that in 2002 both for the whole season 
and for the agriculturally important month of July, the kharif crop production in 
2004-05 was adversely affected by deficient rainfall.

Campaign 2004-05 in September, 2004 which discussed at length the cropping

27.1% of the rural population on the basis of 55th round (1 999-2000) of the 
Household Consumer Expenditure Survey conducted by the National Sample Survey 
Organisation (NSSO). However, the poverty estimates released by the Planning

National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority 
4674. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) the main functions of National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority; 
(b) the steps taken by this Authority to control prices of drugs; 
(c) the details of cases of overcharging by drug manufacturing companies that 
came to light during the last three years; 
(d) action taken against such companies for overcharging; and 
(e) whether Government will make it mandatory for drug manufacturing 
companies to get prior approval for fixing Maximum Retail Price (MRP)? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) to (e) The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) was 
set up by the Government in August, 1997. It has been entrusted with the task, 
inter-alia, to fix prices and notify changes therein, if any, of bulk 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
drugs and formulations, from time to time, under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 
1995 (DPCO, 95). 
In accordance with the provisions of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995, 
(DPC01995) the NPPA fixes/revises prices of the drugs listed in its First 
Schedule and formulations based thereon. In case, there is any violation of the 
approved/notified price of a Scheduled formulation, action is taken under the 
provisions of the DPCO' 1995. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. The Government takes 
corrective measures where the public interest is found to be adversely 
affected. 
Since the inception of the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority 
(NPPA) in August, 1997 and until January, 2005 a demand of Rs. 597 crores 
has been raised for overcharging in 263 cases. Of these, roughly 70% i.e.., in 
184 cases, companies have fully or partly paid the amounts due. Approximately, 
Rs. 83 crores has been recovered so far. 
As per DPCO 1995 provisions, no manufacturer or importer, except those 
exempted, shall market a Scheduled formulation without obtaining the prior 
approval of its price from the Government/NPPA.

Violation of Environment Protection 
Act, 1986 
4695. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have permitted laying of Railway lines and 
drawing of high tension electric cables etc. to pass through forest areas and 
wildlife sanctuary as in case of the Kodagu district of Karnataka implying cutting of 
thousands of trees to create a 100 meter wide corridor for cables; 
(b) whether such acts of omission and commission by Government 
tantamount to weakening and violation of Environment Protection Act 1986; and 
(c) whether such acts open up thick virgin forest areas to human intrusion 
for the first time leading to illegal poaching, logging and other environmentally 
destructive activities? 
104 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) As per information received from 
the Government of Karnataka, no such permission for creation of corridor for laying of 
cables, has been granted in Kodagu District under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. 
However, M/s. Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. has proposed to take up survey work 
for the construction of 400 KV DC transmission line between Mysore and Kozikode 
passing through Kodagu district without involving tree felling. Further, under the provisions 
of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, the Central Government grants 
permission/forestry clearance for implementation of development projects including 
construction of railway lines and laying of transmission lines, on forest land. As per the 
guidelines issued under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, the maximum permissible, 
right of way for laying of transmission lines of 800 KV in forest areas, is 85 metres. 
Diuing implementation of such development projects, minimum felling of trees as per the 
requirement of the project, is invariably involved. 
(b) It is mandatory for all the State/Union Territory (UT) Governments and the 
concerned user agency to seek all statutory clearances prior to taking up any non-
forestry activity on the forest land. There is no question of omission and commission on the 
part of the Central Government in this regard. To undertake any non-forestry activity in 
forest areas, the State/UT Government and the concerned user agency are required to 
take prior permission of the Central Government under Forest (Conservation) Act, 
1980. If the project area falls in a national park/sanctuary, the project proposal, 
inter-alia, requires the recommendation of National Board of Wildlife, and permission 
of the Supreme Court. Alongwith forestry clearance under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. 
if applicable depending upon the nature of the project, the user agency is also required to 
seek environmental clearance under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. 
(c) Conservation and development have to proceed hand in hand, and Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980, is playing a pivotal role in balancing the conservation efforts 
with developmental activities in forest areas of the country. Since implementation of 
development projects on forest lands invariably involves felling of trees, including other 
impacts on environment, the Central Government stipulates specific conditions for 
carrying out compensatory afforestation, wildlife management plans and anti-poaching 
scheme etc., to mitigate the ill-effects arising out of diversion of forest land and 
consequent felling of trees.

Recommendations from the Central Bureau of Investigation 
Short-Term 
(i) With the consent of the State Governments of Rajasthan and Delhi, the CBI

Delhi FIR No. 82/2005 dated 31.01.2005. Any other case arising out of 
incidents of poaching shall also be registered and investigated by CBI for 
which a general consent may be given by the State Governments. 
(ii) Extensive search of all the villages within the Tiger Reserve areas should be 
conducted for recovery of steel traps, guns and other equipments, used for 
killing wild animals. 
(iii) An alert may be issued to all the Tiger Reserves about the modus operandi otthe 
poachers and for recovery of such steel traps, wherever possible. 
(iv) Searches may be conducted in all possible places where steel traps are being 
manufactured and supplied to the poachers.

poaching enforcement operations, in association with Forest Department 
staff.

(vi) Provisions of Section 34 of Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 which requires every 
gun licence holder residing within 10 kms. area of the Sanctuary, to apply to

enforced.

(xi) More than 50% staff of the Tiger Reserve are work charge employees who

Number of elephants in the country 
†4702. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the number of elephants is declining rapidly in the country; 
(b) if so, the figures of number of elephants during the last five years; 
(c) the major steps taken by Government in this regard keeping in view the 
decreasing number of elephants; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The 
estimated population of elephants in the country has shown an increase from 
25,877 in 1997 to 26,413 in 2002 when the last census was carried out. 
(c) and (d) Elephants have been included in Schedule 1 of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972 which prohibits their hunting and also trade in ivory. Export 
of ivory from the country is also banned. India is a signatory to the Convention on 
International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna & Flora (CITES) which 
prohibits international trade in ivory and other elephant products. Government of 
India provides financial assistance under Project Elephant to major elephant-
bearing states in the country for protection of elephants and their habitats and also 
for mitigating human-elephant conflict An amount of Rs. 13.34 Cr. was released 
under the Project during 2004-05. 25 Elephant Reserves have been notified in 
the country for the systematic and focused management of elephants. 
Government of India has also empowered the C.B.I, under the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute the wildlife offenders.

4711. DR. RADHAKANT NAYAK: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state:

Orissa during the last five years; and

districts of Orissa which are predominantly tribals? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) The National Forest Policy, 
1988 envisages to have a minimum of one-third of the total land area of the country 
under forest or tree cover. The approach paper of Planning Commission also 
envisages increase in the forest cover to 25% by the year 2007 and to 33% by 
the year 2012. During the last five years (2000-01 to 2004-05), 135800 hectares

management of these forests in  accordance with Joint Forest 
Management (JFM) concept. 
(iii) Massive plantation programme is being taken up under Nationaf 
Afforestation Programme (NAP) through Forest Development 
Agencies (FDA). In the State 32 FDAs are now functioning and 
27,900 hectares of forest area has been developed during the last two 
years.

districts.

Statement-II 
Action taken Report 
Rural Drinking Water supply is a State subject. Government of India 
introduced the centrally sponsored Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP) in 1972-1973 to accelerate coverage of problem 
villages by rendering financial and technical assistance to States. The entire 
programme was given a mission approach when the National Drinking Water 
Mission (NDWM) was set up in 1986. NDWM was renamed as Rajiv Gandhi 
National Drinking Water Mission (RGNDWM) in 1991. 
2. The primary objective of RGNDWM was to improve the performance and 
cost effectiveness of the on-going programmes in the field of rural drinking 
water supply and sanitation and help ensure availability of adequate quanity of 
drinking water of acceptable quality on a long-term basis. 
3. Rural Drinking Water Supply is largely dependent on ground water (85%). 
Though ground water is less susceptible to pollution as compared to surface water, 
it is affected by the composition of eath's crust. Leaching action of the Arsenic 
bearing rocks at some places leads to occurrence of Arsenic in ground water. 
4. Contamination of ground water with Arsenic was first noticed in 6 
districts in West Bengal in the early 1980s. The first attempt to tackle the 
problem was made in 1988 by sanctioning an investigative study under the R&D 
programmes. Thereafter, several R&D projects as well as field-oriented 
programmes, were sanctioned in the Arsenic affected areas. 
5. At the instance of RGNDWM, the States carried out a survey of quality-
affected habitations in 1991 based on 1% random sampling. As per results of 
this survey, 3,133 habitations in West Bengal were found to be affected with 
arsenic contamination. Another survey in 2 phases was ordered in the year 2000, 
based on 5 to 10% stratified sampling of sources in each Block in Phase-I, 
followed by Phase-ll in which 100% testing of sources was done in the Blocks 
where quality affected sources were found in the Phase I. The West Bengal 
government has reported 4,973 habitations affected with arsenic contamination in 
75 blocks in 8 districts, namely, 24 Parganas South, 24 Parganas North, Malda, 
Nadia, Bardawan, Murshidabad, Hoogly and Howrah. The total population at 
risk in these 75 blocks of 8 districts is estimated as 16 million. 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
6. Among the various techniques developed for removal of arsenic, two methods, viz., (i) 
Co-precipitation technique and (ii) Absorption technique, are the most common. The PHED, 
Government of West Bengal and other organization like. All India Institute of Hygiene and 
Public Health (AIIH&PH), Calcutta and Bengal College of Engineering, Howrah have also 
installed arsenic removal plants in the Arsenic affected aeras of the State. Besides, Domestic 
filters have also been developed by these organizations. A programme of Water Quality 
Monitoring an Surveillance was also launched by RGNDWM by initially setting up State and 
District level Water Quality Testing laboratories to ensure providing safe drinking water 
by the State Governments and generate awareness about water quality among rural 
masses. 17 district laboratories were sanctioned by RGNDWM for West Bengal, out of 
which 13 were established. In the remaining 6 districts, the State Government established 
laboratories from their own sources. One Mobile laboratory was also sanctioned by 
RGNDWM and delivered to West Bengal Government. , 
7. Helping State Governments to tackle water-quality problems in the rural areas is 
one of the objectives of the RGNDWM. Sub-mission programmes were introduced 
in 1992-93 to tackle water quality and sustainability problems. The funding pattern was 
75:25 between Centre and State. Under the Sub-mission programme for control of Arsenic, 
four projects proposed by the State Government were sanctioned during 1994-98 for 
West Bengal by RGNDWM. The West Bengal Government implemented these projects.

Revival of Malaria 
4728. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that reappearance of mosquitoes through out the country 
has resulted in revival of Malaria; 
(b) whether Government have conducted any research on Malaria repellants 
like planting of Marigold flowers or other such measures; if so, the details 
thereof; 
(c) whether inadequate sewerage in cities and towns is one of the factors for 
reappearance of mosquitoes and revival of Malaria; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government have taken do deal with the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) The mosquito nuisance is 
determined by several factors like unplanned urbanization, physical 
environment, life style of the people and water-management system. There are 
several species of the mosquitoes which have different breeding habits. The 
mosquito for spread of malaria i.e. 'Anopheles' usually breeds in clean water. The 
effective control of mosquito can be achieved by environmental modifications & 
manipulations. The National Malaria control Programme was started by the Govt, 
of India in 1953 which was converted to National Malaria Eradication Programme 
in 1958. There was spectacular reduction of malaria incidence as well as deaths. 
However, during late 1970's there was resurgence of malaria due to operational, 
technical and administrative factors. With the introduction of Modified Plan of 
Operation in 1977, the number of malaria cases declined from 6.4 million to 
below 2 million in 2002. Since then the number of cases of malaria has 
remained below 2 million. 
(b) Though there are some reports in literature about the insecticidal 
and repellent activity of the extracts of Tagetus (Marigold), these have not 
been used/studied as malaria repellent by planting of Marigold flowers and 
other plants in the country. 
There is however a report on a study conducted by scientists from Kenya 
and Ethiopia on live potted plants including Tagetus (Marigold) tested as mosquito 
repellent which did not show any significant repellent effect of Tagetus. 
(c) and (d) Bad sewerage system cause breeding of Culex mosquitoes 
151 
 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
but malaria transmitting Anopheles mosquitoes do not breed in sewer water. 
The Govt, of India has a well defined Programme viz. National Vector Borne 
Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) for control of malaria in the country 
adopting strategies which include surveillance, early diagnosis and prompt 
treatment of cases, sustainable vector control including Indoor Residual Spray 
with insecticides treated bednets, use of larvivorous fish etc. besides Training 
& Information, Education and Communication to enlist community 
involvement. Urban Malaria Scheme is also being implemented in 131 Towns 
in the country to reduce density of mosquitoes and to prevent spread of malaria.

Over utilisation of railway tracks 
4773. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether over utilisation of Railway Tracks to the extent of 125 per cent would 
go against Railway Safety; 
(b) whether rejected wagons and coaches are re-used without clearance from the 
NCW; 
(c) whether this kind of rejected wagons and coaches are used almost to the 80 per 
cent to 90 per cent in the Southern Railway; 
(d) the measures to avoid this situation; and 
(e) whether among the railway accidents, it is found that human failure is the highest, 
and the special measures undertaken to curb this kind of failures? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) No, Sir. Over utilization of sectional capacity in some case may lead to 
some what less availability of track for maintenance. However, safety of track is not 
allowed to be affected and in case of need suitable temporary speed restrictions are 
imposed to ensure safety, 
(b) Sometimes, coaches and wagons rejected by Neutral Control Examiner 
(NCE) on account of not carrying out certain modifications, leaving minor deficiencies in 
scale of passenger amenities which do not affect safety, are permitted to be deployed for 
service. Such permission is given judiciously, so as not to detain rolling stock after overhaul 
in workshops, in the interest of overall availability of coaches and wagons for public use. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise. 
(e) Yes, Sir. Safety is the prime concern of Indian Railways ana adoption of new 
measures to improve safety is a continuous process. The measures being taken by Indian 
Railways to minimize incidence of accidents include adoption of suitable modern 
technology for interlocking and signaling systems, up-gradation of track and rolling 
stock, modernization of maintenance practices, replacement of over aged assets, up-
gradation of training aids like simulators, checks on observance of safety precautions and 
provision of Anti Collision Device with continuous and sustained efforts, the number of 
accidents are coming down over the years.

Increasing the Speed of

4780. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that increase in the speed of Shatabdi Express has been put 
on hold; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether Government feel that it may be dangerous to run the fastest trains on the 
Indian Tracks? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
R. VELU): (a) to (c) No, Sir. It was contemplated to increase the maximum speed 
of Shatabdi Express between New Delhi-Agra Cantt section, to 150 kmph. The track 
and signalling system, available on this section, is adequate to run such a train. 
However, the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety (CCRS) has not, so far, 
cleared the running of this train and has drawn attention to issues like provision of fencing 
throughout to prevent cattle straying on to track, train protection and warning system as 
an additional measure to prevent a driver passing signal at danger, provision of frills on 
lifting barrier at level crossing gates as an additional measure to prevent entry of road users 
in a closed gate, Ultrasonic Flaw Detection (USFD) of rails by Self Propelled Ultrasonic 
Rail Testing (SPURT) car in addition to manual testing etc. Action has been taken to 
satisfactorily address all these issues, before the train is run.

Steel Prices 
4793. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: 
SHRI MATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Tata Steel has hiked its long-term contract prices 
by 20 per cent effective from April 1,2005; 
(b) if so, whether other PSUs and Joint Sector Steel Plants are likely to follow 
suit; 
212 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the impact of rise in steel prices on Indian Economy and common man? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) No, Sir. 
With effect from April 1, 2005 Tata Steel has increased the prices of its 
different products by 8-12%. 
(b) and (c) With effect from April 1,2005 Steel Authority of India Limited 
(SAIL) has increased prices of its different products by 6-9% and Rashtriya Ispat 
Nigam Limited (RINL) has increased its prices by 5-6%. The price increase has 
been attributed to the increase in cost of raw materials and strong market 
conditions. 
(d) While there are many institutional factors, which impact the growth otthe 
National Economy, the rising prices of steel, which is mainly used in the 
infrastructure and manufacturing sectors, have not inhibited growth in these 
sectors. During 2002-03, when steel prices registered an average growth of 19% 
over the previous year, the growth in capital formation in steel related segments 
of Construction, Manufacturing, Transport, Storage and Communication and 
Electricity, Gas and Water was 10.42%. 
The rise in steel prices has led to a number of representations from the 
consumer industries. In particular the construction sector, which uses about 
60% of steel produced in the country,  has strongly represented against the 
increase in prices.

4794. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to 
state:

Steel Plant and to install air turbo compressor and oxygen turbo compressor at

revamped. Further, one number of Air Turbo Compressor (ATC) and one number of 
Oxygen Turbo Compressor (OTC) are also proposed to be installed in the Oxygen Plant

Authority of India Limited (SAIL) in March' 2005 at an estimated cost of Rs. 102 crore and 
Rs. 81 crore respectively. The final approval will be accorded after finalization of tenders 
which are in progress. Thereafter, the revamping of Sinter Plant-ll at BSP and one number of

tonnes per annum of pig iron. The ATC and OTC at Bokaro Steel Plant are being installed to

Steel production 
4795. SHRIS. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to refer to 
unstarred Question 607 given in the Rajya Sabha on the 4th March, 2005 and state: 
(a) the details of concrete plan to achieve the target of steel production by over 100 
million tonnes per annum by 2020; 
(b) whether the iron ore reserves of the country are sufficient to meet the target; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the steps proposed to be taken thereon; and 
(d) the role assigned to public sector steel companies in achieving the target 
particularly to Salem Steel Plant? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) The proposed 
National Steel Policy envisages an indigenous production of over 100 million tonnes of 
steel by 2019-20 and seeks to remove the supply-side constraints to the growth of this 
industry in an open, globally integrated and competitive environment in order to achieve the 
goal. After 
214 

[6 May, 2005]                        RAJYA SABHA 
12.00 Noon 
the Policy is approved, a concrete action plan to achieve the given targets 
is expected to be prepared by an empowered Group of Ministers under the 
Chairmanship of the Steel Minister. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) It is estimated that 190 million tonnes of iron ore would be required 
for producing 110 million tonnes of steel by 2019-20. Additional mining 
capacity would be developed to ensure availability of the required quantity 
of iron ore. 
(d) The proposed NSP seeks to remove bottlenecks towards achieving 
the level of growth envisaged by 20 19-20 for the steel sector. While it 
addresses the constraints for growth in the different segments of the steel 
industry, it does not specify growth targets at the plant level.

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Sir, I have great pleasure in 
welcoming this Bill. I had welcomed it most wholeheartedly when it was first 
brought before the House and I am very happy that the hon. Minister has taken 
the earliest opportunity to present the Bill again to this august House for its 
consideration and approval. Many distinguished speakers, 

244 

[6 May, 2005]               RAJYA SABHA 
who spoke before me, spoke about the greatness of this institution. May I say 
that, in my student days, when there were only 21 Universities in the whole of 
India, we had always heard the name of the Allahabad University as topping the 
list of 21. The great Vice-Chancellors of this University, like Amarnath Jha, and 
great scholars, like Ishwari Prasad, were know to students far deep south in 
kerala, when I was a student in my University. But it is also a fact that this 
University lived far too long on its past of glory and during the last quarter of a 
century, at least, 15-20 years, it had been on the decline. Politicisation not only 
at the students level but also at the teachers level, total neglect of research 
and inability to produce men of excellence in various disciplines, which it used 
to do in the past, all these have brought down the reputation if this great University 
and it was delegated to the list of mediocre Universities in this country. That is why 
people like me wholeheartedly welcomed it when the Bill came before the House 
with the hope that a great institution with a great past and a redoubtable future 
could be retrieved from the morass into which it had fallen and made again a 
Centre of Excellence. The Bills is to declare this institution as a Centre of 
National Importance. 
I would like to make three or four points. Before I do that, may I know how 
many minutes are allotted to me? 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: You have got three minutes. 
DR. C.P. ALEXANDER: Agreat discipline that I have learnt after coming to the 
House is to convey ones views within three or four minutes. If I need one or two 
minutes more, I will crave you indulgence. 
The first point that I would like to make is that there should be some criteria 
for accepting further Universities or institutions as Centres of National Importance. I 
am not disputing the claim of the Patna Univesity which was pressed by one 
honb'le member nor am I disputing the claims of other institutions which may 
come up for the consideration of the Minister. But it is necessary that the Ministry 
should lay down some criteria or guidelines for the recognition of an institution as 
a Centre of National Importance. Some Hon'ble members who spoke before 
me.talked about autonomy for universities. But it should be understood that 
when an institution is taken up as a centre of national importance, we should 
allow the Central Government to have a say in its management and the 
ideologies, objectives and programmes on which it should place importance in 
future, so it would be good if the Central Government, that is the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development, has a common Act for all Central universities, 
instead of having separate Acts for each university, as it is today. There is the 
Banaras University; there is the Pondicherry University and there are many 
other

RAJYA SABHA             [6 May, 2005] 
 institutions of national importance. Just as we in Maharashtra brought all 
the 18 or 19 universities of the state under one common Act in 1994 and 
introduced a uniformity regarding Government's control the degree of 
autonomy, etc. it Thus proved to be a great success. It in 1994.I would 
suggest for the consideration of the hon. Minister a uniform Act for all the 
Central institutions. 
The third point is about the selection of the Vice-Chancellor. The existing 
procedures may be all right, but I would suggest that someone should 
interview the candidates who are recommended by the selection panel. If 
the expert panel, comes out with four or five names out of which one 
person is selected. But all Persons recommended by the panel, if I may 
speak based on my experience as the Chancellor of the universities in 
Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu, will have the same type of qualifications on 
paper. They would all have Ph.D. degrees; they would all. have published 
books; they would all have guided research and they would all have done 
25 to 30 years of teaching. Unless you interview a candidate at some level 
to assess not merely his academic merit, but also administrative ability 
through intelligent questions, it would be difficult to have a proper selection. 
At some level of the se lection process, to asse ss the suitability of the 
candidates recommended. There should be an interview and arrive at a 
decision where on person is selected. 
Finally, the Allahabad University should turn out to be a real national 
institution. While it has been nurtured by the State of Uttar Pradesh and it 
represents the culture of the great region of the north, it should develop the 
national character once it is a centre of national importance. There should 
be some guidelines from the Ministry to all institutions of national importance 
as to how they would take up subjects for research on national unity, 
communal harmony, national integration and other such problems which 
plague our country today. I am sure that Allahabad University will make its 
distinct contribution to the development of national unity and integration. I 
wish the University all success in its new avtaar. Thank you.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Meningococcal Disease 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): Sir. meningococcal disease is an acute bacterial disease 
caused by the bacterium Meningococcus and is manifested by sudden 
onset of fever, severe headache, nausea and vomiting, stiff neck and 
frequently a petechial rash with pink  macules and very rarely vesicles 
often accompanied by delirium and coma. Occasionally, fulminating cases 
exhibit severe sudden prostration, ecchymoses and shock at onset. The 
causative agent at present is known to have 12 serogroups. Serogroups 
A, B, C are the commonest and have epidemic potential. Other serogroups 
to name a few W-135, Z, Y, Z etc. are less virulent. 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [6 May, 2005] 
A small proportion of case progress to invasive disease characterised by one 
or more clinical syndromes including bacteraemia. Many with septicaemia 
develop petechial rash. Joints may also be involved. Meningococcaemia 
may occur without meningitis. Out of 25 cases test at the National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases, Delhi, 5 cases have been found positive for 
serigroup a Meningococcal infection. 
As per the information received from the Government of NCT, a total number 
of 91 cases and 14 deaths have been reported till yesterday. Till today, there are 
111 cases and 15 deaths have occurred till today. 
The community is advised to report to the nearest health facility as soon as 
possible if there is sudden rise of high fever along with headache, vomiting, neck 
pain or skin rashes. All major hospitals such as Dr. RML Hospital, Safdarjung 
Hospital, Smt. Sucheta kriplani Hospital, Kalawati Saran Children Hospital, 
AIIMS, LNJP Hospital, G.T.B. Hospital. Hindu Rao Hospital, Deen Dayal 
Upadhyay Hospital, etc., are fully equipped to treat such patients. Hospitals in 
Delhi as well as private practitioners have been advised to notify suspected cases 
to the medical Officer, Municipal Corporation of Delhi (Telephone No. 2393 6101). 
There is no need of panic since the disease is amenable to antibiotic treatment and 
there are sufficient stocks of medicines. Facilities for rapid diagnosis of the 
disease are available at NICD. Ac ontrol room at NICD (Telephone No. 
23981289) will receive the clinical samples round the clock. Guidelines for 
prevention of disease transmission including chemoprophylaxis have been 
provided to concerned health authorities in consultation with WHO. 
The situation is under control and is being regularly monitored.

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, I have only one question. The 
statement mentioned 91 cases have been reported. The number of cases,

DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, I understand the concerns of not only 
the hon. Members but also the general public. I once again want to inform 
the House, through you, that we are looking at the situation and monitoring 
it very carefully. The Central and the State machinery are in full gear in 
these areas. We are carrying out surveys, monitoring and educating the 
public about how we could prevent this. A lot of measures have been taken 
to educate the people through print and electronic media and through 
loudspeakers in various parts of Delhi. At the same time, we do not want 
to create panic among the people. This is not an epidemic-like situation 
today. An epidemic occurred last in Delhi was 20 years ago. 
Now, I come to the queries raised by the hon. Members. Shri 
Narayanasamy mentioned about the short supply of medicines. There are 
two things in this. One is medicine and the other is vaccine. Vaccine is 
for prevention and medicines are for treatment. There is no short supply of 
medicines. Simple antibiotics can treat this. This is just a gram-negative 
bacterium. It is not a viral disease. It is just a bacterial disease and it 
could easily be cured or treated. If anybody has a headache or fever or 
skin rash, with oral antibiotics like cyprofloxacin, refampycin for children 
and injection crystalline penicillin, this can be treated. These are common 
antibiotics available anywhere in the market. These are less expensive 
antibiotics. So, this could easily be cured if we immediately go to hospital. 
But the death occurred because it took  them a little more time—two or 
three days—to go to hospital and, by which time, it became bacteraemia. 
That means, it entered into the blood vessels. 
Coming to the vaccination part, I would say that there is no short supply 
of this. There is sufficient vaccine here. But, at this point of time, vaccinating 
everybody is not required. Vaccination is only required to those people 
who have been engaged with the affected individuals, like the immediate 
relatives. If there are any symptoms of this disease then the people who 
258 

[6 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
are surrounding the patient should be vaccinated before one, two or three 
days and the people who are living in mass areas like hostels or jails 
where they live together without much hygiene, they should be immunised. 
So, general public need not be immunised and that is not necessary as it 
is today. As far as Haryana is concerned, the Haryana Government has 
put it on alert as it shares border with Delhi. It is good on their part to take 
preventive steps. 
The increase in the number of patients, reflects suspected cases, 
yesterday, the number of cases was 91; today it is 111. Yesterday there 
were 14 deaths; today there are 15 deaths. We are concerned about each 
and every single death. That's our concern. We don't want anybody to die. 
We are watching the situation very closely. 
Hon. Member, Shri Jairam Ramesh, has asked about the causes in the 
Capital. Sir, this bacteria, Neisseria meningococcal, is prevalent in about 
15-20 per cent of all the individuals in the pharynx, in the larynx and in the 
upper respiratory tract throughout the year. But when there is a conducive 
atmosphere, there is an outbreak. The bacteria goes to the brain and it 
become meningitis. If it goes down in the body, it becomes 
meningococcaemia. And, .neningococcaemia is even more potent. There 
are a lot of kits that are readily available. The National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases has put a lot of kits. These kits have been supplied 
to all the municipal workers, all the doctors, and all the hospitals. It is very 
easy to detect this disease. We are trying to evaluate the sensitive hot 
spots. The WHO is assisting us to evaluate that. There are more incidents 
of cases in the old city because it is very congested and lacks hygiene 
and sanitation. This disease is, in fact, transmitted through a droplet. 
When you cough there is a droplet. When you go near a patient, it is not 
that the droplet is prevalent at some point of time. Since it is a bacterium, 
it is very vulnerable. It is a very hi ghly sensitive bacterium. It does not 
remain there in the air for a long time. So, people need not panic about 
that. 
So far as preventive measures are concerned, both the Delhi Government 
and the Central Government are living up to the situation. Today also we 
had a high-level meeting at about 12.30 P.M. All the officials had attended 
the meeting. It is not that we had a meeting today only, rather we are 
having a meeting everyday. We are closely reviewing the situation so that 
it does not get out of control. We are putting it in the newspapers, we are 
putting it on the television for the public as to how to be careful. If they 
have some headache or fever, they should consult a doctor immediately. 
Unlike the other viruses, this can easily be treated.

A question had also been put about the treatment facilities. Sir, as I 
mentioned, all the hospitals, whether Government or private, are treating that. 
We had also asked the Municipal Corporation of Delhi to notify this disease. So,

Then, Mr. Nariman had raised a point, should a private medical 
practitioner be consulted? Sir, we  have the National Institute of

effective antibiotics like Ciprofloxacin, Cefriaxone Injection and Rifampicin are 
available. All the antibiotics are available. 
A question was raised why in the last three days the Government has not 
taken any steps. We have taken a lot of steps not only during the last three days, 
but also from the beginning. We have been taking a lot of steps in this 
regard. 
Was there any preparation to stop this epidemic? Yes, Sir. After this, we are 
going through the programme called Integrated Disease Surveillance Project. The 
Government has taken up the Project. This is, approximately, a Rs. 400-crore 
World Bank funded Project. So, in three years time, we are going to have this

last years. 
I now come to the demand for vaccine. There is absolutely no shortage. There is 
no shortage of vaccines. We have sufficient vaccines. The NICD has sufficient 
vaccines. We have talked to private manufactures also. Them is a company in

company called, Advences. They are private m anufacturers. They have

SHRI VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY): Now, we take

DR. KARAN SINGH (NCT OF DELHI): Sir, I move:— 
"That the Bill to provide for securing a life with dignity, peace and 
security to the aged and for their welfare and for matters connected 
therewith, be taken into consideraton." 
Sir, in our tradition, we have a well-established principle that looking 
after elderly parents is considered to be an act of great merit, a great 
punya: िजन मात-िपता की सेवा की, तीन तीथर्-ĭत िकयो न िकया, 
meaning, if somebody who has looked after his parents, it doesn't 
matter whether he has done extensive pilgrimages or kept fasts; he 
has fulfilled his karma. This is something built into our tradition. 
However, I would like to draw your attention, Sir, to the fact the di 
Sankaracharya, writing 1400 years ago in one of his strotas, has a very 
telling verse:

meaning, as long as you have wealth, everydody asks about our welfare,

of the Adi Sankara, it meant that both things continued in our society. 
There was a strong feeling that you should look after the parents; but 
there must also have been cases in which parents were grossly neglected 
and mistreated. 
Now, Sir, with the inevitable break-up of the joint family and the emergence 
of the nuclear family, the position of elders has become more precarious 
than before.The joint family, with all its shortcomings and weaknesses, 
nonetheless, did provide some kind of a security network for those who 
were elderly and for those who were incapacitated. But, now, with the 
families breaking up, and the responsibilities coming directly on the children, 
the situation is beginning to change. Many hon. Members in this House 
must have seen recently a film called Baghban where Amitabh Bachchan 
and a colleague of ours in the Rajya Sabha portrayed an elderly couple 
and the way their children treated them. That is a film that everybody 
should see because it carries within it, in a very dramatic, in a very moving 
manner, the way in which elderly people now are thirsting for affection and

Sir, elderly people face a whole barrage of problems. They face financial 
insecurity because, very often, they are not in pensionable jobs. It is not 
always possible for them to be insured. Therefore, they are dependent 
upon their children or upon their relatives, and financial security is something 
that strikes at the very root of dignity and of self-respect. They face physical

with those problems specifically which are faced by people, as they grow 
old. As the body grows older, certain problems develop. And above all, Sir, 
it is the psychological insecurity which is the most dangerous because 
psychologically the elders do not want pity. They want dignity; they want 
their self-respect. And if that is denied to them, then, it becomes a very 
painful situation. So, whether it is financial security, physical security, 
healthcare, psychological security, it is very important that special measures 
should be taken.

face multiple problems. In our country, we have not yet developed a network

homes for the elderly, where people are prepared to pay a modest amount

developed in our country. And, I would suggest, Sir, that NGOs should be 
encouraged to undertake these sorts of ventures. There are organisations 
like Helpage India.Rotary, Lions Club and so on. 
Sir, religious trusts have vast sums of money at their disposal, and they 
should really be the pioneers in this. Let me give you the example of the 
Sikh community, which runs free l angars always. You will never see a 
Sikh beggar on the road because the Sikh community is a community

Unfortunately, the bulk of the population is not covered either by governmental 
schemes or by NGOs and religious trusts. Therefore, something urgently 
needs to be done to look into these problems of the elderly. 
Sir, it is true that the Budget has  provided some concessions to the 
elderly, as far as taxes are concerned and travel and so on are concerned. 
But, very much more needs to be done the United Nations adopted in 
1991 what they called the U.N. Princi ples for Older Persons, and they 
urged all national Governments to include them in their programmes. There 
are many principles. But there are five particularly, to which I would like to 
draw the attention of the hon. House. Independence: Older persons should 
have access to food, water, shelter, clothing, health care, work and other 
income generating opportunities, education, training and life-enhancing 
environment. Participation: Older person should remain integrated into the 
community life and participate actively in formulation of policies affecting 
the well-being of the nation. Care: Older person should have the access to 
social, legal services and to health care so that they maintain optimum 
level of physical, mental and emotional well-being. This should include full 
respect for dignity, beliefs, needs and privacy. Self-fulfilment: Older person 
should have access to education, cultural, spiritual and rcreational resourcs 
and be able to develop their full potential. And, finally, dignity: Older person 
should be able to live in dignity and security and be free from exploitation 
and physical or mental abuse and be treated fairly regardless of age, 
gender, social or ethnic background.

is an issue on which the Government needs to pay far greater attention 
than it has in the past. Whether it wants to make the extension of social 
security a challenge for public exchequer, but implemented through a variety 
of organisations like NGOs, Civil Society Organisations, Self-Help Groups, 
panchayats, is an issue that I think the Government will have to grapple 
with. Sir, I think, it is true that a large number of fiscal inventives are, in 
fact, being provided to the aged. The Finance Minister has made some 
concessions to senior-citizens. The Railways, the Indian Airlines and so 
on and so forth also have a variety of schemes for senior citizens. The 
problems of seniors citizens and the aged have been coming on to the 
public domain, but I think, what it requires is a far more coordinated and 
integrated approach than has been the case so far, involving social welfare, 
involving education, involving health, involving security. Dr. Karan Singh 
has raised the issue of the aged being, particularly, vulnerable to the 
problems of insecurity, particularly, in towns, and cities, and I think these 
are all issues that have to be dealt with in a coordinated manner. If the 
National Commission is able to do this, then, I think, it is a worthwhile 
steps. But, I think, we should draw  lessons from previous National 
Commissions. We have a National Commission on Women; there is a 
Bill, Sir, for a National Commission on Children; now, there is a Private 
Member's Resolution for a National Commission on the Aged. I think, we 
need to address ourselves on the questions, not so much on the National 
Commission on the Aged, the need for it is incontrovertible, but how it is 
going to be structured, who is going to man this National Commission, 
and what are the instruments that are going to be given to it to implement 
its mandate, etc. These are some of the more important questions that 
arise, so that we make the National Commission a more effective 
instrument, not only of raising consciousness in our society of the problems 
of the aged and the senior citizens, but more importantly, of getting 
Government action across a variety of fronts, both on the part of the Central 
Government as well as on the State Government. Sir, with these few words, 
I would tend to support Dr. Karan Singh's proposal for the setting up a 
National Commission for the Aged. Thank You.

PROF. P.J. KURIAN: Sir, I have to make only one point The old-age 
people are now becoming a problem for our society. What is the basic 
reason? The basic reason is the cultural invasion of the West. Our great 
tradition and culture is that we consider our parents and old people as
